summary.text: A residue-class sieve modulo \(30030=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\), with \(\varphi(30030)=5760<30030/5\), gives \(\pi(5M)\le M\) for \(M\ge10^6\); absorbing smaller values into \(C_0=\pi(5\cdot10^6)\) then inductively bounds every term by the maximum of \(C_0\) and the initial values. Thus the five-term windows range over a finite set, so two coincide by pigeonhole, and determinism of the recurrence propagates that equality forever to give a positive eventual period.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\pi(x)\) denote the number of primes at most \(x\). Given initial values
\[
v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\in \mathbb N,
\]
define \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) by
\[
a_i=v_i\quad(0\le i<5),
\]
and, for every \(i\ge 0\),
\[
a_{i+5}=\pi(a_i+a_{i+1}+a_{i+2}+a_{i+3}+a_{i+4}).
\]
We prove that this sequence is ultimately periodic. In fact, the proof works for arbitrary nonnegative initial values, so the stipulated positivity of the five initial values is more than is needed.

We begin with an elementary uniform estimate for the prime-counting function.

Define \(\pi_{<}(N)\) to be the number of primes strictly less than \(N\). Thus
\[
\pi(x)=\pi_{<}(x+1).
\]
Certainly
\[
\pi_{<}(N)\le N,                                                    \tag{1}
\]
since the primes below \(N\) form a subset of \(\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}\).

We will use the modulus
\[
q=30030=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13.
\]
Because these six prime factors are distinct, Euler's totient function gives
\[
\varphi(q)
=(2-1)(3-1)(5-1)(7-1)(11-1)(13-1)
=1\cdot2\cdot4\cdot6\cdot10\cdot12
=5760.                                                        \tag{2}
\]

We record the elementary sieve estimate underlying the proof. If \(q\ne0\), \(k>q\), and \(t\ge0\), then
\[
\pi_{<}(k+t)
\le \pi_{<}(k)+\varphi(q)\left(\left\lfloor\frac{t}{q}\right\rfloor+1\right). \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, split the primes below \(k+t\) into those below \(k\) and those in the half-open interval \([k,k+t)\). If a prime \(p\) belongs to the latter interval, then \(p\ge k>q\). It follows that \(p\) is coprime to \(q\): otherwise, since \(p\) is prime, \(p\) would divide \(q\), which is impossible when \(p>q\). Thus the number of primes in \([k,k+t)\) is no larger than the number of integers in that interval that are coprime to \(q\). In each complete block of \(q\) consecutive integers, exactly \(\varphi(q)\) integers are coprime to \(q\), and an incomplete final block contributes at most another \(\varphi(q)\). There are at most \(\lfloor t/q\rfloor\) complete blocks and one possible incomplete block. This proves (3).

We now derive a convenient global linear estimate:
\[
\pi_{<}(N)\le 35791+5760\left\lfloor\frac{N}{30030}\right\rfloor
\quad\text{for every }N\ge0.                                  \tag{4}
\]
If \(N\le30030\), this follows immediately from (1), because
\[
\pi_{<}(N)\le N\le30030<35791
\]
and the second term on the right of (4) is nonnegative.

Suppose instead that \(N>30030\), so \(N\ge30031\). Apply (3) with
\[
q=30030,\qquad k=30031,\qquad t=N-30031.
\]
Using (1) and (2), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{<}(N)
&\le \pi_{<}(30031)
 +5760\left(\left\lfloor\frac{N-30031}{30030}\right\rfloor+1\right)\\
&\le30031+5760
 +5760\left\lfloor\frac{N-30031}{30030}\right\rfloor\\
&=35791+5760\left\lfloor\frac{N-30031}{30030}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(N-30031\le N\), monotonicity of integer division by a positive integer gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{N-30031}{30030}\right\rfloor
\le \left\lfloor\frac{N}{30030}\right\rfloor,
\]
and (4) follows.

The purpose of (4) is the following contraction estimate:
\[
M\ge1{,}000{,}000\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \pi(5M)\le M.       \tag{5}
\]
To check this carefully, put
\[
r=\left\lfloor\frac{5M+1}{30030}\right\rfloor.
\]
Because \(\pi(5M)=\pi_{<}(5M+1)\), estimate (4) yields
\[
\pi(5M)\le35791+5760r.                                         \tag{6}
\]
Also, by the defining property of the floor,
\[
30030r\le5M+1.                                                  \tag{7}
\]
Multiplying (7) by \(5760\) and adding \(30030\cdot35791\), we get
\[
30030(5760r+35791)
\le5760(5M+1)+30030\cdot35791.
\]
The right-hand side is at most \(30030M\) whenever
\[
5760(5M+1)+30030\cdot35791\le30030M,
\]
or equivalently
\[
30030\cdot35791+5760\le1230M.
\]
Here
\[
30030\cdot35791+5760=1{,}074{,}809{,}490,
\]
whereas \(M\ge1{,}000{,}000\) gives
\[
1230M\ge1{,}230{,}000{,}000.
\]
Thus the required inequality holds. Since \(30030>0\), cancellation gives
\[
5760r+35791\le M.
\]
Together with (6), this proves (5).

We next turn (5) into an estimate valid for every \(M\). Set
\[
C_0=\pi(5{,}000{,}000)=\pi(5\cdot1{,}000{,}000).
\]
We claim that
\[
\pi(5M)\le\max\{M,C_0\}\quad\text{for every }M\ge0.            \tag{8}
\]
If \(M\ge1{,}000{,}000\), this follows from (5), since \(M\le\max\{M,C_0\}\). If \(M<1{,}000{,}000\), then \(5M\le5{,}000{,}000\), so monotonicity of \(\pi\) gives
\[
\pi(5M)\le\pi(5{,}000{,}000)=C_0\le\max\{M,C_0\}.
\]
This proves (8).

Now define
\[
V=\max\{v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\}
\quad\text{and}\quad
B=\max\{V,C_0\}.
\]
We prove that every term of the sequence is bounded by \(B\):
\[
a_n\le B\quad\text{for every }n\ge0.                           \tag{9}
\]
We use strong induction on \(n\). For \(0\le n<5\), this is immediate from \(a_n=v_n\le V\le B\). Now let \(n=i+5\), and suppose that (9) has already been proved for all indices less than \(n\). In particular,
\[
a_i,a_{i+1},a_{i+2},a_{i+3},a_{i+4}\le B,
\]
so
\[
a_i+a_{i+1}+a_{i+2}+a_{i+3}+a_{i+4}\le5B.
\]
By the recurrence and monotonicity of \(\pi\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i+5}
&=\pi(a_i+a_{i+1}+a_{i+2}+a_{i+3}+a_{i+4})\\
&\le\pi(5B)\\
&\le\max\{B,C_0\},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last inequality is (8). But \(C_0\le B\) by the definition of \(B\), hence \(\max\{B,C_0\}=B\). Therefore \(a_{i+5}\le B\), completing the strong induction and proving (9).

It remains to use this boundedness and the deterministic nature of the recurrence.

For every \(n\ge0\), form the five-term state
\[
S_n=(a_n,a_{n+1},a_{n+2},a_{n+3},a_{n+4}).
\]
By (9), each coordinate of \(S_n\) belongs to the finite set
\[
\{0,1,\ldots,B\}.
\]
Consequently there are at most \((B+1)^5\) possible states. The infinite list
\[
S_0,S_1,S_2,\ldots
\]
therefore contains a repeated state: by the pigeonhole principle there exist distinct nonnegative integers \(m,n\) such that
\[
S_m=S_n.                                                        \tag{10}
\]
After interchanging \(m\) and \(n\) if necessary, assume \(m<n\). Thus (10) says
\[
a_{m+j}=a_{n+j}\quad(0\le j<5).                               \tag{11}
\]

We show that equality of these two five-term windows propagates forever:
\[
a_{m+k}=a_{n+k}\quad\text{for every }k\ge0.                   \tag{12}
\]
This follows by strong induction on \(k\). For \(k=0,1,2,3,4\), it is exactly (11). Suppose now that \(k=i+5\), and that the assertion is known for every smaller offset. The five induction hypotheses at offsets \(i,i+1,i+2,i+3,i+4\) give
\[
a_{m+i+j}=a_{n+i+j}\quad(0\le j<5).
\]
Applying the recurrence at indices \(m+i+5\) and \(n+i+5\), respectively, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{m+i+5}
 &=\pi(a_{m+i}+a_{m+i+1}+a_{m+i+2}+a_{m+i+3}+a_{m+i+4}),\\
a_{n+i+5}
 &=\pi(a_{n+i}+a_{n+i+1}+a_{n+i+2}+a_{n+i+3}+a_{n+i+4}).
\end{aligned}
\]
The five summands in the first expression equal the corresponding five summands in the second, so the two values are equal. This completes the induction and proves (12).

Finally, take
\[
N=m,\qquad P=n-m.
\]
Because \(m<n\), we have \(P>0\). If \(r\ge N=m\), put \(k=r-m\), so that \(r=m+k\). Since \(n=m+P\), equation (12) gives
\[
a_r=a_{m+k}=a_{n+k}=a_{m+P+k}=a_{r+P}.
\]
Thus
\[
\forall r\ge N,\qquad a_{r+P}=a_r,
\]
with \(P>0\). Hence the sequence is ultimately periodic, as required.
